opus-5.5.text:
Initially, honestly, there was a period of adjustment. You're bringing together two organizations that each had their own cultures, their own infrastructure, their own codebases, and even their own ways of thinking about research. Brain had grown up very close to Google's production systems and had this fairly bottom-up, researcher-driven culture, while DeepMind had a more top-down, mission-oriented style with big coordinated projects. So in those first months, a lot of energy went into just figuring out how to work together: which training stack do we standardize on, how do we organize teams, who owns what.

But I think the bigger effect, even early on, was focus. Before the merger, there was a fair amount of duplicated effort. You had parallel efforts on large language models, on infrastructure, on evaluation, and compute was split across them. Once we came together, the decision was essentially: let's pool our compute, pool our people, and put a lot of that behind one flagship model effort. That was a big shift. It meant some people had to let go of projects they cared about, which isn't easy, but it also meant that when you got a training run going, you had the best people from both sides looking at the data, the architecture, the evals.

So I'd say in the very short term there was some friction, and maybe a little bit of time lost to reorganization. But fairly quickly the pace picked up, because instead of two groups each running somewhat smaller efforts, you had one much larger, more coordinated push. And the combination of strengths mattered: Brain brought a lot of depth in things like Transformers, large-scale training, and infrastructure close to TPUs, and DeepMind brought a lot of experience in reinforcement learning, in running very ambitious, tightly managed projects. Putting those together, I think, ended up accelerating things more than either could have managed alone.

r001.rationale: The response says the groups had to figure out how to work together across different cultures and systems, causing short-term friction and some time lost to reorganization before the pace picked up. This communicates unfamiliarity working together as a possible cause of an initially slower development pace.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in the very beginning it slowed things down a little, and I think anyone who was there would tell you the same. You had two organizations that had been, in a friendly way, competing for years. Different codebases, different infrastructure stacks, different cultures around how you run an experiment or make a decision. DeepMind had a more centralized, long-horizon research style, and Brain had been very bottom-up, with lots of small teams exploring things on their own. So the first few months were a lot of figuring out who owns what, which training stack we standardize on, how we even talk about compute allocation.

But that friction was front-loaded. Once the Gemini effort really consolidated, the pace picked up dramatically, and I think faster than either side could have managed alone. The big thing was that we stopped duplicating work. Before the merger, you'd have two or three teams independently building large models, each getting a fraction of the available compute and a fraction of the people. After, you had one flagship effort with the best infrastructure people from both sides, one data pipeline, one evaluation suite everyone trusted. That concentration mattered more than almost anything else.

The other piece people underestimate is talent mixing. You'd put someone who'd spent years on reinforcement learning at DeepMind next to someone who'd spent years scaling transformers at Brain, and they'd have arguments that neither group had internally. A lot of the post-training work, the reasoning work, came out of exactly those collisions.

So my short answer is: a brief slowdown while we paid down the integration cost, and then a real acceleration. If we'd stayed separate, I don't think we'd have shipped at the cadence we did.

r001.rationale: The response says the organizations had competed for years and describes their different codebases, infrastructure, and cultures as sources of the initial slowdown, communicating that they lacked experience working together.

astra-6.text: I think initially there’s a coordination cost when you bring two large research organizations together. You have to align priorities, decide how teams will work together, and get people working toward a shared goal. So I wouldn’t expect the immediate effect to be that everything suddenly moves faster. But the longer-term opportunity is to bring complementary expertise together and reduce duplicated effort. I’d distinguish that initial adjustment period from the pace you can achieve once the teams are aligned.

r001.rationale: The response describes coordination costs and an initial adjustment period, but does not identify the teams’ lack of prior experience working together as a possible cause of slower model releases.
